concepts.name: Aurobindo's Early Life, Education at Cambridge and Return to India
key_dimensions: ICS examination: qualified but deliberately missed the riding test to avoid selection — significance of this deliberate act
Exposure to European nationalism (Mazzini, Irish nationalism) and its influence on his political thought
Contrast: Western education yet rejection of colonial modernity — how this shaped his unique nationalist position
Service under Baroda State (1893–1906): dual role as administrator and clandestine revolutionary organizer

concepts.name: Aurobindo's Doctrine of Passive Resistance vs. Active Resistance
key_dimensions: His 1907 writings distinguishing passive resistance from Gandhian non-violence — not identical concepts (UPSC trap)
Passive resistance as a weapon of the weak that can escalate: Aurobindo's view that it is a transition, not an end
Contrast with Moderate school: Moderates sought reforms within empire; Aurobindo demanded complete Swaraj by any means
Why Aurobindo criticized petitioning and 'mendicancy politics' of the early Congress

concepts.name: The Four-Fold Programme: Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott, and National Education
key_dimensions: Aurobindo's intellectual authorship and articulation of these four pillars before the 1905 Partition agitation formalized them
His specific conception of Swaraj as complete independence (not dominion status) — distinguishing him from Tilak's occasional ambiguity
National Education as an alternative to colonial knowledge systems — link to his later educational philosophy at Pondicherry
How the four pillars were operationalized in Bengal during 1905–08 and their limitations

concepts.name: Aurobindo and the Extremist (Garam Dal) Faction: Surat Split of 1907
key_dimensions: Role of Aurobindo alongside Tilak and Lajpat Rai in consolidating the Extremist bloc before Surat
The specific procedural dispute at Surat — presidency question (Rash Behari Ghose) and the shoe-throwing incident
Consequences: British repression targeted Extremists; moderates gained control of Congress machinery till 1916
UPSC trap: Aurobindo was the ideological architect but Tilak was the more prominent face — distinguishing their roles

concepts.name: Yugantar and Kal Newspaper: Aurobindo as a Revolutionary Journalist
key_dimensions: Yugantar (founded 1906): open advocacy of armed revolution — contrast with Bal Gangadhar Tilak's Kesari (more coded)
Bhawani Mandir pamphlet and Doctrine of the Sword: philosophical justification of violence as sacred duty
British legal response: sedition charges, press prosecutions — how Aurobindo used the courtroom as a political platform
Distinction between Yugantar (Bengali, mass-oriented) and Karmayogin (English, intellectual audience) — different phases of his activism

concepts.name: Anushilan Samiti and Yugantar Group: Aurobindo's Role in Secret Revolutionary Societies
key_dimensions: Aurobindo as one of the key organizers of the Anushilan Samiti network — distinction between Calcutta and Dhaka branches
His brother Barindra Kumar Ghosh's operational role vs. Aurobindo's ideological/organizational role — UPSC often conflates the two
Link between revolutionary societies and the broader Swadeshi movement: complementary but distinct strategies
Yugantar group's activities: political dacoities, arms procurement, bomb-making — the Muzaffarpur bomb case connection

concepts.name: Alipore Bomb Case (1908–09): Trial, Defense, and Transformation
key_dimensions: Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki's Muzaffarpur bomb attempt (targeting Kingsford) as the trigger for arrests
Aurobindo's arrest and the role of approver Narendra Nath Goswami — his subsequent assassination by fellow revolutionaries in jail
Chittaranjan Das's brilliant defense argument: 'In the prisoner... India of the future takes shape' — political significance of the trial
Acquittal of Aurobindo but conviction of Barindra — why this outcome and its effect on Aurobindo's political trajectory

concepts.name: The Uttarpara Speech (1909): Spiritual Nationalism and Its Political Implications
key_dimensions: Context: delivered shortly after release from Alipore jail — public declaration of spiritual transformation in prison
Key thesis: nationalism as a divine mission, India's role as vishwaguru — conflation of political and spiritual liberation
Criticism: did the spiritual turn represent a retreat from political struggle or a deeper philosophical reframing?
UPSC angle: contrast with contemporaries — Gandhi's also spiritualized politics but through ahimsa; Aurobindo through shakti and activism

concepts.name: Aurobindo's Concept of 'Nationalism as Religion': Ideology and Critique
key_dimensions: Drawing on Hindu philosophical traditions (Shakti worship, Bhagavad Gita's karma yoga) to legitimize revolutionary action
Bhawani Mandir pamphlet (1905): Mother India as goddess Bhawani, revolution as spiritual sadhana
Criticism from secular nationalists and Muslim leaders: religionization of politics and its exclusionary implications
Comparison with Tilak's use of Ganesh Puja and Shivaji festivals — similar instrumentalization of religion for nationalism

concepts.name: Aurobindo's Reinterpretation of the Bhagavad Gita in Political Context
key_dimensions: Essays on the Gita written during Alipore imprisonment — karma yoga as justification for political violence
Contrast with Gandhi's interpretation of the Gita as advocating non-violence (allegorical reading)
How colonial authorities viewed his Gita writings: seditious philosophy cloaked in scripture
Long-term influence: his Gita commentary became foundational to his integral yoga philosophy post-1910

concepts.name: Aurobindo's Flight to Pondicherry (1910) and Its Political Significance
key_dimensions: Immediate trigger: fresh warrant in the Howrah Gang Case (1910) — not a voluntary spiritual retreat initially
Pondicherry as French territory: beyond British jurisdiction — strategic, not merely spiritual choice (UPSC trap)
Political criticism: abandonment of the nationalist movement at a critical juncture vs. his claim of divine instruction
Effect on the revolutionary movement: leaderless, suppressed by 1910 — Morley-Minto Reforms partly a response to contain extremism

concepts.name: Karmayogin and Dharma Newspapers: Intellectual Phase of Aurobindo's Activism
key_dimensions: Karmayogin (English weekly, 1909–10): targeted educated Indian audience with philosophical nationalism
Open Letter to My Countrymen in Karmayogin: rejected Morley-Minto Reforms as inadequate — continued political stance post-Alipore
Dharma (Bengali): parallel vernacular publication for wider reach
British seizure of Karmayogin offices and the resulting warrant — direct link to his Pondicherry flight

concepts.name: Aurobindo's Critique of the Morley-Minto Reforms (1909)
key_dimensions: His argument: separate electorates for Muslims were a deliberate divide-and-rule strategy — prescient analysis
Rejection of the reforms as 'illusory concessions' that left sovereign power intact with the British
Contrast with Moderate response: Gokhale and Naoroji cautiously welcomed the reforms as a step forward
UPSC relevance: understanding the spectrum of nationalist responses to constitutional reforms

concepts.name: Aurobindo's Views on Indian Unity and Communal Harmony
key_dimensions: His vision of Indian nationalism as inclusive of all religions under a civilizational (not Hindu communal) identity
Tension: his use of Hindu symbolism while claiming a composite national identity — contemporaries' skepticism
His later writings from Pondicherry on Hindu-Muslim unity and the need to transcend religious divisions
Contrast with V.D. Savarkar's Hindutva — both emerged from revolutionary nationalism but diverged sharply on communal question

concepts.name: Aurobindo vs. Bal Gangadhar Tilak: Similarities, Differences, and Complementarity
key_dimensions: Similarities: both Extremists, both used religion for nationalism, both advocated Swaraj and Boycott
Key difference: Tilak remained in active politics till death (1920); Aurobindo withdrew to Pondicherry in 1910
Ideological divergence: Tilak was primarily a political strategist; Aurobindo evolved into a philosopher of spiritual evolution
UPSC trap: both are called 'father of Indian unrest' — actually this title is specifically associated with Tilak (by Valentine Chirol)

concepts.name: Aurobindo vs. Bipin Chandra Pal: The Bengal Extremist Intellectual Triangle
key_dimensions: Pal, Aurobindo, and Tilak as the 'Lal-Bal-Pal' trio — but Aurobindo's distinct role as the primary Bengal ideologue
Pal's concept of 'spiritual nationalism' and overlap/difference with Aurobindo's formulation
Both Pal and Aurobindo eventually withdrew from active politics — compare their trajectories and reasons
Aurobindo's deeper philosophical systematization vs. Pal's more journalistic and oratorical nationalism

concepts.name: Aurobindo's Pondicherry Phase: Sri Aurobindo Ashram and Integral Yoga
key_dimensions: Political significance of the Pondicherry phase: continued indirect influence through writings even during Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience
His correspondence during 1920s–40s on Indian independence — not entirely apolitical
August 15, 1947 significance: Indian independence on his 75th birthday — his radio address articulating vision for India
Distinction between his political nationalism (pre-1910) and philosophical nationalism (post-1910): continuity vs. rupture debate

concepts.name: Aurobindo's Vision of Complete Independence (Purna Swaraj) and Its Legacy
key_dimensions: Aurobindo articulated Purna Swaraj as early as 1906–07 — predates the Congress's formal Purna Swaraj resolution of 1929 by over two decades
His argument that Dominion Status was incompatible with true freedom — validated by the 1929 Lahore Congress position
Legacy: influenced later revolutionaries like Bhagat Singh ideologically, though they differed on spirituality
UPSC trap: the 1929 Purna Swaraj declaration is associated with Nehru/Gandhi — Aurobindo's prior articulation often overlooked

concepts.name: British Repression of Revolutionary Nationalism and Aurobindo's Legal Encounters
key_dimensions: Sedition Law (Section 124A IPC) as the primary tool: Aurobindo charged multiple times — demonstrates British legal strategy
The Alipore case as a showcase trial: British attempt to decapitate revolutionary movement by targeting its ideological leader
Deportation without trial under Regulation III of 1818 used against others — Aurobindo's acquittal was exceptional
How legal repression inadvertently created martyrs and amplified revolutionary appeal — Aurobindo's acquittal speech and its nationwide impact

concepts.name: Aurobindo's Historiographical Position: Assessment by Historians
key_dimensions: Bipin Chandra's assessment: Aurobindo as the most important intellectual of the Extremist school who provided coherent ideology to revolutionary nationalism
Criticism from Marxist historians (e.g., R.P. Dutt): his spiritualization of politics deflected from class-based analysis
Post-colonial reassessment: Partha Chatterjee on the inner/outer domain distinction in nationalist thought — Aurobindo exemplifies the 'spiritual inner domain'
UPSC angle: ability to compare different historiographical schools' treatment of Aurobindo — nationalist, Marxist, Subaltern
